This is the setup I use to get an AI agent to do a whole PCB. Not help me in KiCad, actually do it. Pick the parts, write the netlist, place everything, route it, output gerbers a fab will build. I review, it does the work.

All of it is public now, and so is the board I'm going to use as the example the whole way through, so nothing here is a claim you have to take on trust. Clone it, run four commands, and you get the same output I did.

## The board

A power and I/O demo shield for the Arduino UNO Q. Screw-terminal input at 7–24 V behind reverse-polarity protection, a TPS54331 buck making 5 V for shield loads, an INA226 monitoring the whole stack's current and bus voltage over I²C, four BSS138 level-shift channels between the UNO Q's 3.3 V headers and 5 V peripherals, Qwiic passthrough, an RGB status LED. Four layers, top side only, 24 BOM lines.

It is deliberately boring, and it is deliberately not a toy. A switching converter sits a few millimetres from a 0.5 mm pitch part, inside the UNO form factor — which fixes the outline, the four mounting holes and all 32 header pins before you place anything of your own. Every rule in its config exists for a reason you can point at on the board: the buck's exposed pad is its only real heatsink, VIN carries up to 4 A, and the UNO Q's Wi-Fi antenna sits directly under the top-left corner, so copper there detunes the radio.

Those coordinates aren't mine. The outline, the hole pattern, the header positions and the antenna keepout were extracted from Arduino's own documents and fab data for the UNO Q, © Arduino SA, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 . Pulling the hole pattern out of the manufacturer's drill file rather than a drawing is the kind of thing this whole method is about.

Where a number below came off a different board, I say so. The method came out of an earlier project, a small data logger — MCU module with Bluetooth, two sensors, a GNSS receiver, storage, USB-C charging, about 60 parts — and several of the scars in here were earned there and paid for in fabricated boards.

Here's the whole thing.

## The design lives in a CSV, not in KiCad

> The schematic isn't the source of truth. A CSV is. The KiCad project is a build output.

One row per pin, every pin of every IC, NC written out where a pin is meant to be unconnected, and a note column that carries the citation. Real rows from this board:

Net,RefDes,Pin,PinName,Note VIN_RAW ,J1,2,VIN, 7-24 V in, matches UNO Q DC_IN range (ABX00162 datasheet 3.2 p.11) VIN_PROT ,Q5,1,S, protected rail out (AO4407A.pdf p.1: pins 1-3 S) GND ,U2,2,A0, address 0x40 = A1:GND A0:GND (INA226 Table 6-2) BOOT ,U1,1,BOOT, bootstrap; 100nF to PH (ds front-page application circuit)

One script turns that into a schematic. Another turns the schematic into a board. Nothing in the KiCad files gets touched by hand. To change the circuit you edit a row and rebuild.

The reason this matters: KiCad files are s-expressions full of coordinates. An agent editing them directly is working on geometry it can't see, in a format where being slightly wrong looks exactly like being right. Nothing errors out. You just get a broken board.

### The round trip check

The schematic generator reads back the file it just wrote, pulls the netlist out of it, diffs that against the CSV, and fails the build if anything doesn't match.

This is the single most important line of the build. An LLM writing KiCad files will eventually put a label a fraction of a millimetre off a pin. The schematic looks perfect. The net isn't there. ERC reads it as an intentional floating label. DRC doesn't look at schematics at all. Without the round trip check you find out when the board comes back and the part doesn't show up on the bus.

## Requirements come out of documents

> An LLM's memory of a pin map is a guess that looks like a fact.

Before any wiring, the agent writes down what the hardware has to provide, and every line carries a citation to something it actually read in that session. Not a recollection, not a plausible number. A document, a page, a table.

This board had no firmware yet, so every requirement came out of Arduino's own material: the datasheet with page numbers as printed, the full pinout, the schematics by sheet number, and the fab data inside their CAD files — the Allegro gerbers and NC drill they actually manufacture from. Sixteen requirements, each with a source. A few of the load-bearing ones:

- All shield-facing logic is 3.3 V. A0 and A1 aren't 5 V tolerant in any mode, and one digital pin is 3.6 V max even in digital mode — which is why the level shifters are the point of the board rather than a nicety

- The shield I²C bus already has 2.2 kΩ pull-ups on the UNO Q itself, found on schematic sheet 20, so the shield adds none. Two boards' worth of pull-ups on one bus is a classic way to get a marginal bus nobody can explain

- The Wi-Fi antenna occupies a specific rectangle in the top-left corner, extracted from the copper in Arduino's own gerber and confirmed against a 600 DPI render. That rectangle becomes the keepout, on all copper layers, pads included

- The four mounting holes are Ø3.2 mm NPTH at coordinates taken from the manufacturer's drill file, not from a drawing. They're fixed by the UNO pattern — not ours to choose

When firmware does exist, it's the best requirements source you have, and the agent should read it first. On the data logger that's where bus addresses, sample rates and partition sizes came from, each cited to a file and a line number. That board also had a headless code path already, so a variant with no display and no I/O expander needed no new code at all, just a pin map. Nothing makes a new board cheaper than finding out the firmware already supports it.

The agent then reads every datasheet against the connection table. This is where it earns its keep, because a BOM with the right ICs on it is usually still missing everything that makes them run. On the data logger that meant a charger with no load-share path, which reads system load as charge current and trickles the cell forever; no battery sense divider on a board whose firmware reports a battery percentage over Bluetooth; a GNSS receiver with no antenna connector and no RF front end; and IMU pins floating, which sits the part in the wrong interface mode so it never answers.

### Have it do the capacity math

Same session, before layout. On this board that's a worst-case VIN current of 3.6 A at the low end of the input range, designed to 4 A, which IPC-2221 turns into a 2.0 mm conductor at 1 oz external copper for a 10 °C rise. The shunt is 10 mΩ, so 4 A puts 40 mV across it — 49% of the INA226's ±81.92 mV range, which is the right place to sit. Inductor ripple works out at 0.69 A peak to peak worst case, so peak current is 1.9 A against a 3.2 A saturation rating.

The number that changes a design is the one that comes out wrong. On the data logger the logging rate was 21 MB/hour into an 896 kB filesystem, which is two and a half minutes of recording. That's why that board has a microSD socket.

Make it show the arithmetic, and make it write down what it rejected. This board's plan names six parts it didn't use and why: a buck in a package with no exposed pad, which would have deleted the thermal-via lesson the board exists to teach; a current monitor whose 26 V absolute maximum is too close to a 24 V nominal input, because an unloaded 24 V supply drifts above it; a one-chip level shifter whose edge-rate accelerators misbehave on exactly the breadboard wiring a first-time user will do. A rejection with a reason is worth more later than the choice itself.

## What I use

### Harness

Claude Code . Four things matter:

- Shell and file access across the whole repo , firmware included.

- Subagents , so part research and layout and firmware work run at the same time.

- Persistent memory. A board takes weeks. What you find on Tuesday has to still be there when you plan the next revision on Thursday.

- A plan doc per revision in the repo: what's in scope, what defect it fixes, how, and a list of checks that have to pass before you order. That last list is the important one.

### Skills

Eleven of them, all from kicad-happy by Andrew Klofas. MIT licensed, works with Claude Code and Codex. This is the install that matters most.

/plugin marketplace add aklofas/kicad-happy /plugin install kicad-happy@kicad-happy

Two things these are good for.

Part selection with the whole picture in it. Every line on this board was checked against JLCPCB's own component endpoint on the day it was signed off: price, stock, and whether the part is Basic or Extended, which is a real cost because each Extended line carries a loading fee. On the data logger the same habit found the expensive version of that problem — a $16.31 part with a seven week lead, whose obvious replacement had more stock but a 22 week lead. The agent found a third option at $2.93, in stock, and gave the reason it worked: the firmware only used three things from the original part, and the replacement puts all three out of its own fusion block. That swap deleted 11 parts, a crystal, half the fanout pads and one layout constraint.

Land patterns out of the drawing, not the text. On this board the RGB LED's common anode is pin 2, which you only learn from the land drawing on page 8. On the data logger a chip antenna's datasheet text said two terminals while the land drawing in the same PDF showed three pads, because the feed terminal sits on a split pad pair. A two pad footprint ships a dead antenna on a board that's otherwise fine.

> The text and the drawing in a datasheet can disagree, and the drawing is what the factory builds. Pull the figure.

### CAD and the toolchain

kicad-tools by RJ Walters. MIT licensed Python toolkit built for agents. Every command outputs JSON and none of it needs KiCad running. It ships an MCP server and a kct CLI, so the agent calls it as tools and the build scripts call the same things. I use it for checkpoint and restore, board inspection, schematic to PCB, the placement tools, zones, and export. I route with Freerouting instead of the built-in routers.

All the headless stages run in one container now, so none of it has to be installed by hand: KiCad 10 on a digest-pinned base image, Freerouting 1.9.0 fetched by checksum, a pinned kct , and uv holding the Python environment still.

git clone https://github.com/ramalamadingdong/pcb-agent && cd pcb-agent python3 scripts/doctor.py # names every missing piece and the fix make setup # builds the image, fetches the pinned jar make build route export check # this board, end to end

Install KiCad natively as well if you want to look at a board — the container has no GUI, and the one X11 thing inside it is a virtual framebuffer that exists solely because Freerouting asks for a screen size it never uses. Match the major version to the boards you build. A KiCad 9 pcbnew loading a KiCad 10 board returns None , with no error and no message.
